headline: Robot policies are getting explicit structure around the frozen model (revisable memory, failure probes judged by what they let you fix, and human data transferred as contacts), while new benchmarks show that spatial language from people is still where VLAs break.
thesis: Today's strongest manipulation results do not come from retraining the policy. Memory is being rebuilt as an auditable record with evidence links that can withdraw stale conclusions, and failure handling is judged by whether an alarm or probe leads to a useful intervention rather than by detection accuracy. World-model ideas are moving into training: predict the future to shape the policy's features, then skip or shrink that prediction at deployment. Human demonstrations transfer when they are expressed as contact goals, wrist-centred hand structure or latent actions rather than raw joint angles. On the human side, a real-robot benchmark finds VLAs execute the motions but lose spatial descriptions out of distribution, and interpretability work points to viewpoint transformation as the bottleneck, which is exactly what a robot needs when a person says "to my left". For a team building robots that talk with people of different ages and cultures, the practical move is to test spatial and perspective-dependent language explicitly, and to measure motion smoothness near people as its own outcome.

clusters.title: Manipulation memory is becoming an explicit, evidence-linked record that can retract conclusions, not a longer frame buffer
clusters.why: The default for memory-dependent tasks has been to feed more history frames to the VLA. Today REMM separates an append-only evidence log from revisable task state and withdraws completed conditions when supporting facts change (2610.12710), GAMMA has VLM agents write one grounded text line per replan window and verifies every claim against detector evidence (2610.12793), a dual-stream design splits execution progress from selective frame retrieval (2610.13262), and MeMoREval finds stored frames beat generated text descriptions, with scene graphs best overall (2610.12561). All four keep the low-level policy fixed or separate. For long tasks that a person can disturb (moving an object, undoing a step), store evidence and derived state separately so the robot can tell what to redo.

clusters.title: Failure handling is measured by whether it enables a useful intervention, and robots are starting to gather the missing evidence themselves
clusters.why: Failure monitors have mostly been scored on separating failed from successful runs. RESCUE replays checkpoints counterfactually and shows that good detection scores do not imply lower intervention cost, with an ideal detector tolerating only a 2.0-3.3% false-alarm rate under stop-and-reset (2610.13516). Fly-by-Code synthesizes diagnostic View and Probe programs when feedback is ambiguous (2610.12549), BT-Agent and EndoRSI turn structured failure feedback and failed physical rollouts into the next revision (2610.13862, 2610.13376), Robot-WATCHDOG detects semantic failures from object graphs learned on nominal runs (2610.13403), and MAGMA-Bench shows planners still degrade under injected failures (2610.13534). When choosing a monitor, evaluate it together with the recovery action you actually have, and budget false alarms against the cost of stopping.

clusters.title: Future prediction is moving to train time: policies learn from predicted futures and then skip or shrink that prediction when deployed
clusters.why: World-action models have paid for future prediction at every inference step, and errors in the predicted video leak into actions. FDM conditions future prediction on action features so ground-truth futures supervise the policy but are never generated at inference (2610.13117), IG-VLA internalizes its imagined future into a single gist token and cuts latency from 1081 ms to 169.5 ms per chunk (2610.02626), Evo-World supervises with optical flow instead of full images in a 0.87B model (2610.12936), SmolWAM reads out actions and future latents in one rectified-flow step at 57 ms (2610.13740), and LeWAM predicts in a JEPA latent space and plans 32.3 times faster than prior JEPAs (2610.12818). For on-robot compute, a predictive auxiliary loss looks like the cheaper way to get most of the benefit.

clusters.title: Human demonstrations transfer to robots as contacts, wrist-centred hand structure or latent actions, not as retargeted joint angles
clusters.why: Retargeting human poses joint-by-joint has been the standard bridge, and it loses what made the task succeed. PanTact records where and when the body touches things and lets the G1 choose which surface realizes each contact (2610.12558), VICAR treats world-frame contact poses and clearance as high-priority terms during retargeting (2610.13079), Human2Dex shares one wrist-centric corpus across two dexterous hands, raising success from 26.3% for raw human data to 85.8% (2610.13119), LAPT-Scale learns continuous latent actions from 23.3K hours of egocentric video (2610.13732), EgoReveal learns where to move the camera from egocentric demos (2610.12999), and ATHLETE combines generic locomotion data with tennis videos (2610.13572). If you collect human data, record contacts and timing explicitly; they survive the embodiment gap better than poses.

clusters.title: Spatial and perspective-dependent language is the weak link between what people say and what VLAs do
clusters.why: VLA evaluations have mostly varied objects and scenes and reported aggregate success. Spa-Bench holds objects and motions in distribution and finds success falls from 67.5-73.3% to 40.7-52.0% on unseen spatial configurations, while rephrasing as direct instructions recovers 28.3-40.0 points (2610.12696). S-Space finds MLLMs encode object coordinates linearly but fail at the transformations needed across viewpoint changes, and couple cardinal with image-relative directions (2610.13527). SpatialASM trains perspective-taking explicitly (2610.13832), and a Stroop-paradigm study shows VLMs systematically favour text over colour cues in the same image (2610.12650). For a robot taking instructions from people, test relational, ordinal and speaker-relative phrasing ("my left", "the second one") as a separate suite, and expect failures there before motor failures.

clusters.title: Generalist policies are adapted through small modules or anchored representations while the pretrained weights stay frozen or constrained
clusters.why: Fine-tuning a VLA on new task data tends to erase what it learned in pretraining. Noise space learning keeps a flow-matching VLA fixed and learns only a context-conditioned noise distribution, with PPO, SAC and AWR variants (2610.13943), Dream to Remember steers a frozen policy and rehearses earlier tasks in a frozen world model, holding CALVIN success at 74.8% where LoRA drops to 11.7% (2610.13816), and RARA anchors fine-tuned representations to retrieved pretraining examples for a 13.6-point out-of-distribution gain (2610.13578). For a fleet that keeps learning new site tasks, a frozen base plus small per-task modules is likely easier to validate and roll back.

insights: Test spatial language separately from manipulation skill. Spa-Bench (2610.12696) shows the evaluated VLAs can do the motion but lose the referent when the spatial configuration is new, and S-Space (2610.13527) points to viewpoint transformation as the internal bottleneck. For a robot serving people across ages and cultures, who phrase locations differently and often speak from their own viewpoint, add an evaluation set of relational, ordinal, counting and speaker-relative instructions on your own robot, and log whether a rephrased direct instruction fixes the failure.

Measure motion quality near people as its own outcome. JitterVLA (2610.13628) shows that irregular, delayed VLA command arrival produces jerky motion even when the predicted action is reasonable, and that simple interpolation cut modeled p99 jerk by 83% on human motion at a 2.0 cm tracking cost. Before running a user study with a VLA-driven arm, replay identical command streams through your controller options and compare jerk; perceived safety in HRI likely depends on this more than on task success.

Stop scoring failure detectors on AUROC alone. RESCUE (2610.13516) finds that favourable detection scores did not establish lower intervention cost and that recoverability depends on the state and intervention pair. Pair each monitor with the recovery you actually run (pause and ask a person, retry, reset) and estimate the false-alarm rate your workflow can tolerate; for robots working among people, an unnecessary stop is also a social cost.

When a person is in the loop, revisable memory is the piece to prototype first. REMM (2610.12710) reports that intervention recovery rose from 57% to 91% in mean task progress by withdrawing conclusions that an operator's disturbance invalidated, without retraining the executor. That pattern (evidence log, derived state, targeted recovery at skill boundaries) maps directly onto a behaviour-tree or ROS 2 action layer.

must_read.why: It isolates spatial grounding from motor skill on a real arm, which is the failure a human-facing robot will hit first when people give relational or ordinal instructions.
must_read.key_idea: Keep objects, concepts and actions in the training distribution and vary only the spatial configuration, then add diagnostics for wording, object-task association and recognizing that no action is needed.
must_read.evidence: 4,092 episodes on an SO-101 arm (1,200 teleoperated demos, 2,892 evaluation rollouts from five VLAs); for three fully evaluated policies, success drops from 67.5-73.3% in distribution to 40.7-52.0% out of distribution, and matched direct instructions add 28.3-40.0 points.
must_read.caveat: Six tabletop tasks on one low-cost arm with instructions from the benchmark authors; it does not test speaker-relative or culturally varied phrasing, so the gap for real users may be larger or different.

must_read.why: It gives a cheap, repeatable way to check whether a VLA-driven arm moves smoothly enough near people before you spend time on a user study.
must_read.key_idea: Replay identical command and arrival traces through different controllers so the controller's effect on jerk is isolated from the policy and the network delay.
must_read.evidence: Synthetic reaches, hand trajectories from 20 people, three open VLA pipelines (838 episodes) and a UR3; interpolation lowered modeled p99 jerk by 83% (615 to 106 m/s^3) at 200 ms delay with a 2.0 cm tracking cost, replicated on 598 new episodes; on the UR3 accelerometer-derived jerk fell 3.0-14.0% in six exploratory pairs.
must_read.caveat: Physical results are exploratory on one arm, and a position-derived metric did not resolve the contrast; no human perception or comfort ratings are reported, so the link to perceived safety is inferred.

must_read.why: If you are adding a failure monitor to a deployed VLA, this changes how you should pick and tune it.
must_read.key_idea: Evaluate a monitor by counterfactually branching from checkpoints and asking whether acting on its alarm lowers expected task-completion cost, not by how well it classifies failures.
must_read.evidence: OpenVLA-OFT and pi0.5 on LIBERO-Spatial and LIBERO-Plus with 128,340 counterfactual branches; 14 of 66 OpenVLA-OFT/LIBERO-Plus failures are recoverable under continuation versus 34 of 66 with scripted recovery; an idealised detector can afford only 2.0-3.3% false alarms under stop-and-reset.
must_read.caveat: Simulation only, on LIBERO variants, with a specific stop-and-reset cost model; real-robot reset costs and human-in-the-loop recovery are not modelled.

must_read.why: It shows a concrete supervisory layer that lets a frozen VLA recover after a person disturbs the task, which is the normal situation for robots working around people.
must_read.key_idea: Separate an append-only evidence history from revisable task state, link each derived condition to its supporting facts, and withdraw and repair only what a new observation invalidates.
must_read.evidence: 51 physical trials with a frozen G0.5 VLA executor, including operator-assisted runs; mean recorded task progress over the strongest baseline rises from 57% to 91% in intervention recovery and from 43% to 70% in sequence recall.
must_read.caveat: Small trial count, some runs operator-assisted, and progress rather than full task success is the reported metric; generality beyond the tested task set and executor is not shown.

must_read.why: It is the clearest version today of getting world-model supervision without paying for future generation on the robot.
must_read.key_idea: Condition future-state prediction on action features (never the reverse), so ground-truth futures shape the policy during training, prediction errors cannot flow into actions, and the future branch is dropped at inference.
must_read.evidence: Instantiated with both VLM and video-generation backbones; 99.4% average success on LIBERO and absolute gains of up to 13% over VLA and WAM methods on real-world tasks.
must_read.caveat: The abstract does not describe the real-world tasks, robots or number of trials, and LIBERO is near saturation, so the size of the real-robot benefit is hard to judge from the abstract.

2610.12710.problem: Long-horizon manipulation memory keeps observations but cannot tell which completed steps a later disturbance has invalidated.
2610.12710.method: A supervisory layer over a frozen VLA that links derived conditions to supporting evidence, withdraws them when evidence changes, and schedules targeted recovery at skill boundaries.
2610.12710.why: Gives a retraining-free way to recover after people move things or undo steps, which maps onto a behaviour-tree layer.

2610.12793.problem: Single VLMs reasoning over hundreds of raw frames hallucinate and fail to turn episodic memory into grounded subgoals.
2610.12793.method: Two VLM agents write and read an append-only text memory grounded by a SAM-3 detector, with a propose-verify harness checking every claim against visual evidence.
2610.12793.why: Shows that auditing memory writes against perception recovers much of the oracle ceiling with the policy held fixed.

2610.13262.problem: Memory-dependent manipulation needs both execution progress and visual evidence that is no longer in view.
2610.13262.method: A Gated DeltaNet compresses history into one temporal token while a task-conditioned retriever keeps relevant frames as spatial tokens.
2610.13262.why: Raises real-robot success from 37.5% to 62.5% on four tasks, and its cup-swap failures flag identity tracking as still open.

2610.12561.problem: It is unclear what embodied agents should store as memory: text descriptions, frames, or structured scene data.
2610.12561.method: MeMoREval separates an experience phase from later information and action requests, scoring success and inference cost across 53 tasks.
2610.12561.why: Suggests storing frames plus scene graphs rather than generated captions for robots that must answer questions about what they saw.

2610.13516.problem: Failure monitors are judged on detection accuracy even though a late or unnecessary alarm can make outcomes worse.
2610.13516.method: Counterfactual branching from simulator and policy checkpoints to test whether acting on alarms reduces expected task-completion cost.
2610.13516.why: Changes how a team should select and threshold runtime monitors for deployed VLAs.

2610.12549.problem: Coding agents refine robot programs from execution feedback that, on aerial manipulators, often hides whether the task succeeded or why it failed.
2610.12549.method: When feedback is ambiguous, the agent writes separate diagnostic programs in simulation that look from new viewpoints or probe physical hypotheses.
2610.12549.why: Raised success from 31.7% to 75% in simulation and suggests robots should actively collect evidence before declaring a task done.

2610.13862.problem: Running LLM agents onboard mobile robots needs responsive, safe execution on limited compute.
2610.13862.method: An onboard 9B model makes task decisions while predefined behaviour-tree skills enforce conditions and return structured failure feedback.
2610.13862.why: A pattern that fits ROS 2 stacks directly, with ablations showing structured tool calls and failure feedback matter most.

2610.13376.problem: Robot-policy research still relies on engineers to interpret physical failures and decide how to revise controllers.
2610.13376.method: A human-governed coding agent revises endoscopic robot policies using evidence from safety-constrained physical experiments.
2610.13376.why: Shows physical failures falsifying an offline-supported strategy, with insertion success rising from 2/21 to 17/21 over four generations.

2610.13403.problem: Failures cannot be enumerated in open-world manipulation, and image-based detectors miss semantic and interaction errors.
2610.13403.method: Self-supervised object-centric spatio-temporal graphs scored by trajectory projection and a graph-attention forecaster trained on nominal runs only.
2610.13403.why: A failure detector that needs no failure labels and catches interaction-level errors image methods miss.

2610.13534.problem: Benchmarks rarely test long-horizon multi-robot planning under execution failures, interruptions and mission updates together.
2610.13534.method: An architecture-agnostic skill-level benchmark with controlled online perturbations and heterogeneous robots, plus 261,646 training examples.
2610.13534.why: Even the strongest models fail on many clean episodes, a warning for LLM task planners on mixed fleets.

2610.13117.problem: VLAs lack supervision from future states, while WAMs pay inference cost and let visual prediction errors leak into actions.
2610.13117.method: Future prediction is conditioned on action features so it supervises the policy during training and is skipped at inference.
2610.13117.why: Gets world-model supervision without on-robot generation cost, across both VLM and video-model backbones.

2610.02626.problem: Explicit future rollouts at every VLA step are too slow for deployment.
2610.02626.method: Learns to imagine future scene evolution in representation space, then internalizes it into a compact Scene Gist Token used at inference.
2610.02626.why: Keeps the benefit of future reasoning while cutting per-chunk latency from 1081 ms to 169.5 ms.

2610.12936.problem: Future-image prediction entangles task-relevant motion with static appearance and is heavy for VLAs.
2610.12936.method: Supervises a lightweight VLA with future optical flow and decouples representation learning from action optimization.
2610.12936.why: A 0.87B model that outperformed evaluated baselines on real AgileX single-arm and bimanual tasks with lower memory use.

2610.13740.problem: Strong world-action models rely on video diffusion transformers that are too heavy for edge devices.
2610.13740.method: Prunes and re-interfaces a 2B Cosmos Policy trunk to read out actions and future latents in one rectified-flow step.
2610.13740.why: 57 ms per 16-action chunk with 2.4 GiB GPU memory makes a WAM plausible on robot-class hardware.

2610.12818.problem: JEPA pipelines train representations, dynamics and policy separately, which limits planning quality and speed.
2610.12818.method: Jointly trains next-latent prediction and action flow matching with an isotropic Gaussian latent constraint so one model both acts and plans.
2610.12818.why: One model supports direct execution and fast sampling-based planning, reported 32.3 times faster than prior JEPAs.

2610.12558.problem: Humanoid manipulation is limited to the hands because body-contact demonstrations are hard to capture and transfer.
2610.12558.method: A wearable interface with contact patches records body contact locations and timing; the robot chooses which surfaces realize each contact goal.
2610.12558.why: Enables pushing, sweeping and load-sharing with the whole body on a G1 from robot-free human demonstrations.

2610.13079.problem: Video-to-humanoid imitation loses the world-frame contact poses and timing that define contact-rich tasks.
2610.13079.method: Retargets human video motion with high-priority Lagrangian terms for contact poses and clearance, then trains a contact-conditioned motion generator.
2610.13079.why: Lets a humanoid adapt learned skills such as table-tennis serves and ladder climbing to new contact positions at runtime.

2610.13119.problem: Every dexterous hand normally needs its own task demonstrations.
2610.13119.method: A wrist-centric human demonstration interface with a shared 21-point hand representation and grasp-pocket object encoding, retargeted per hand.
2610.13119.why: One human corpus reached 90.8% and 80.8% success on two different hands, against 26.3% for raw human data.

2610.13732.problem: Egocentric human video lacks robot action labels, and existing latent action models lose fine motion detail.
2610.13732.method: Continuous latent actions learned from 23.3K hours of video with perceptual, semantic and optical-flow alignment, used to pre-train a VLA.
2610.13732.why: Real-robot success rose from 63.3% to 85.0% as annotated human video grew from 1K to 5K hours.

2610.12999.problem: Egocentric-demo methods ignore that manipulated objects are often partially occluded.
2610.12999.method: Two imitation policies, one for camera-arm repositioning and one for manipulation, switched by target visibility.
2610.12999.why: Shows active viewpoint choice can be learned from cheap human demos, useful for cluttered homes.

2610.13572.problem: Reactive humanoid tennis needs motion data covering many approach states that is costly to capture.
2610.13572.method: Combines generic locomotion with video-derived strokes via trajectory-guided motion matching, then teacher-student distillation and PPO.
2610.13572.why: Real forehand and backhand hit rates of 90.00% and 86.67%, including rallies with human players.

2610.12696.problem: VLA evaluations report aggregate success and leave spatial grounding of language untested.
2610.12696.method: A real-robot benchmark that varies only spatial configuration across six task types, with diagnostics for wording and no-action recognition.
2610.12696.why: Shows the evaluated VLAs lose spatial referents out of distribution, a key risk for robots taking instructions from people.

2610.13527.problem: It is unknown how multimodal language models internally represent space and where their spatial reasoning fails.
2610.13527.method: Identifies a linear subspace encoding object coordinates and uses causal interventions and direction-word readouts to diagnose failures.
2610.13527.why: Points to viewpoint transformation and mixed reference frames as the bottleneck for perspective-dependent instructions.

2610.13832.problem: LVLMs do not spontaneously take other viewpoints when reasoning about space, unlike people.
2610.13832.method: Trains active spatial mentalization with generated novel views and automatically built perspective-taking tasks.
2610.13832.why: Perspective-taking is what a robot needs to resolve speaker-relative directions in conversation.

2610.12650.problem: It is unclear how VLMs choose between conflicting features in one image.
2610.12650.method: Adapts the psychological Stroop task to VLMs and traces the text-over-colour bias to representation and steering asymmetries.
2610.12650.why: A psychology-grounded probe showing VLM perception has systematic salience biases that a human-facing robot inherits.

2610.13943.problem: Adapting VLAs to specific tasks must respect limited interaction, compute and safety budgets.
2610.13943.method: Keeps a flow-matching VLA fixed and learns a context-conditioned noise distribution with PPO, SAC or AWR.
2610.13943.why: Gives practical recommendations for which adaptation variant to use under different deployment constraints.

2610.13816.problem: Steering or fine-tuning generalist policies on sequential tasks causes catastrophic forgetting.
2610.13816.method: Rehearses earlier tasks through imagined rollouts in a frozen world model while a steering module learns the new task.
2610.13816.why: Supports continual site-specific learning without a replay buffer, including on a real Franka.

2610.13578.problem: Few-shot fine-tuning of pretrained policies distorts their representations and hurts out-of-distribution robustness.
2610.13578.method: Aligns target-demo representations with retrieved pretraining examples and limits their drift during fine-tuning.
2610.13578.why: Reported 13.6-point out-of-distribution gain over plain fine-tuning with Diffusion Policy and GR00T.

2610.13628.problem: Delayed, irregular VLA command arrival can make a robot move abruptly near people even when the action is reasonable.
2610.13628.method: A replay benchmark that pushes identical command and arrival traces through alternative controllers to isolate their effect on jerk.
2610.13628.why: A screening step before human-centred studies, showing interpolation sharply lowers jerk at small tracking cost.

2610.12706.problem: Fear of falling keeps many older adults from exercise, and walkers or exoskeletons are bulky or stigmatized.
2610.12706.method: A soft wearable skirt of pressurized pneumatic pouches that can support the full body weight, with on-board pressure sensing.
2610.12706.why: An assistive design centred on acceptability for older users, though fall testing used a single user.

2610.12772.problem: Humanoids struggle to react with the whole body to moving objects using only egocentric vision.
2610.12772.method: Three-stage learning: state-based whole-body catching, dynamics inference from delayed observations, then an RGB-D encoder for that representation.
2610.12772.why: Catches human-thrown boxes on a real G1, a concrete case of reactive physical interaction with people.

2610.13945.problem: Generalist VLAs fail in a user's own home or office without costly local demonstrations.
2610.13945.method: A phone scan builds a Gaussian-splat digital twin, auto-generates pickup tasks and oracle demos, and fine-tunes pi0.5 in two stages.
2610.13945.why: Raised pickup from 0% to 62.5% in the target scene and 63.9% on a real Stretch 3, a path to per-home personalization.

2610.12832.problem: VLAs need robot-action pretraining and extra action heads to turn VLMs into policies.
2610.12832.method: Projects a TCP-centred action frame into the wrist camera image and expresses actions as native VLM text output.
2610.12832.why: Suggests zero-shot manipulation from a plain VLM with a path to fine-tuning in the same action space.

2610.13788.problem: LiDAR-inertial odometry degrades in smoke and dust, and degradation is rarely labelled.
2610.13788.method: An LSTM autoencoder trained only on nominal data scores LiDAR reliability and switches localization to radar-inertial odometry.
2610.13788.why: A practical pattern for graceful sensor fallback in degraded environments, with code to be released.

2610.13838.problem: Flipper controllers for tracked robots rely on elevation maps corrupted by odometry drift under the chassis.
2610.13838.method: A mapless controller using IMU, flipper angles and a short-window motion cue to stabilize and free the robot.
2610.13838.why: Traversed a log hidden in grass that stopped the best map-based controller.

2610.13158.problem: Map-based collision queries cost too much preprocessing for millisecond reactive avoidance.
2610.13158.method: A GPU ESDF query computed directly on posed depth images, integrated into an MPC.
2610.13158.why: Lower latency and memory than voxel grids on embedded GPUs, relevant to reactive avoidance on any mobile base.

2610.13354.problem: Learning-based assembly relies on demonstrations, task decomposition and dense rewards.
2610.13354.method: Trains one policy from scratch on all 20 NIST board tasks with only a sparse binary reward and task diversity.
2610.13354.why: 98.2% training success in simulation with emergent regrasping and ordering behaviour, though real-robot transfer is not reported.

2610.12957.problem: Embodied product agents must adapt to product constraints, changing goals and execution failures.
2610.12957.method: A ReAct-style VLM agent trained on sandbox trajectories with goal revisions and failure recovery, then distilled and RL-tuned.
2610.12957.why: Quadruped case studies show replanning and explicit failure reporting, useful behaviour for user-facing robots.
